title: Introduction to Security
subtitle: Climb the money ladder — one security question per grade level

questions.q: The CIA Triad is the foundation of information security. What does the 'A' in CIA stand for?
options: Authentication
Authorization
Availability
Accountability
questions.note: Availability means authorized users can access data and systems when needed. Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability are the three pillars of the CIA Triad.

explain.correct: Availability ensures that systems and data are accessible to authorized users whenever they need them. A denial-of-service attack, for example, violates availability.
wrong: Authentication is the process of verifying identity — it is part of access control, not a pillar of the CIA Triad.
Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to do — also not a CIA Triad pillar.
Accountability (audit logging and non-repudiation) is a security concept but is not one of the three CIA Triad components.

questions.q: Security experts now recommend prioritizing password LENGTH over complexity. Which of the following is the BEST password practice according to modern NIST guidelines?
options: Change your password every 30 days regardless of breach
Use a short password with uppercase, numbers, and symbols
Use a long passphrase of 16+ characters that you can remember
Reuse the same strong password across multiple accounts to remember it
questions.note: NIST SP 800-63B (2017) shifted guidance away from forced complexity and periodic rotation toward length — passphrases of 15+ characters are significantly harder to crack. Reuse and short passwords remain high-risk.

explain.correct: NIST SP 800-63B recommends length over complexity. A 16-character passphrase has far more entropy than a short complex password and is also more memorable.
wrong: NIST 800-63B explicitly discourages mandatory periodic password changes unless there is evidence of compromise — forced rotation leads to predictable patterns like 'Password1!' → 'Password2!'.
Short passwords are far easier to brute-force regardless of character complexity. Length provides exponentially more entropy.
Reusing passwords across accounts is one of the most dangerous practices — a single breach exposes every account that shares that credential (credential stuffing).

questions.q: An attacker follows an authorized employee through a secured door without badging in, gaining access to a restricted server room. What is this physical attack called?
options: Shoulder surfing
Tailgating
Dumpster diving
Vishing
questions.note: Tailgating (also called piggybacking) exploits social courtesy — employees hold doors open for people who look like they belong. A mantrap (double-door airlock) is the primary physical countermeasure.

explain.correct: Tailgating occurs when an unauthorized person physically follows an authorized person through a secured entry point without using their own credentials. Mantraps prevent this by allowing only one person through at a time.
wrong: Shoulder surfing is observing someone's screen or keypad to steal PINs or passwords — it does not involve physical door access.
Dumpster diving is searching through discarded materials (paper, drives) for sensitive information — no door bypassing is involved.
Vishing is voice-based phishing over a phone call — it is a social engineering attack, not a physical intrusion method.

questions.q: Which type of malware is UNIQUE in that it can self-replicate and spread across a network entirely on its own, WITHOUT needing to attach itself to an existing file or program?
options: Virus
Trojan
Worm
Spyware
questions.note: A worm is standalone and self-propagating — it exploits network vulnerabilities to spread automatically. A virus requires a host file; a trojan disguises itself as legitimate software but does not self-replicate.

explain.correct: A worm self-replicates and propagates across networks without any user interaction or host file. The 2003 SQL Slammer worm infected 75,000 servers in 10 minutes by exploiting a SQL Server vulnerability.
wrong: A virus requires a host file or program to attach to and needs user action (opening the infected file) to execute and spread — it cannot travel on its own.
A trojan disguises itself as legitimate software to trick users into installing it. It does not self-replicate or spread on its own.
Spyware silently monitors user activity (keystrokes, browsing) and reports it to an attacker. It does not self-replicate or spread autonomously.

questions.q: An attacker sends a fraudulent text message to an employee claiming their corporate account is locked and asking them to click a link to reset their credentials. What type of social engineering attack is this?
options: Phishing
Vishing
Smishing
Pretexting
questions.note: Smishing = SMS phishing. The delivery channel defines the attack type: email = phishing, voice call = vishing, text/SMS = smishing. All three are social engineering attacks that create urgency to manipulate victims.

explain.correct: Smishing is phishing conducted over SMS (text messages). The attack uses urgency ('your account is locked') to pressure victims into clicking malicious links or surrendering credentials.
wrong: Phishing uses email as its delivery channel, not SMS text messages. It is the most common form of social engineering overall.
Vishing (voice phishing) uses phone calls or voicemail — not text messages — to manipulate victims into revealing information.

Pretexting is the creation of a fabricated scenario (a 'pretext') to manipulate a target — it is a technique that can underlie phishing, smishing, or vishing, but is not the specific attack name here.

questions.q: A user logs into a VPN by entering a password AND approving a push notification on their smartphone. Why does this qualify as Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)?
options: Because two separate passwords are required
Because the login uses two steps, regardless of factor type
Because the password and the phone represent two DIFFERENT factor categories
Because MFA always requires a biometric scan as the second factor
questions.note: MFA requires factors from at least two DIFFERENT categories: Something You Know (password), Something You Have (smartphone/token), Something You Are (biometric). Two passwords = two 'know' factors = NOT MFA — that is just two-step verification within one category.

explain.correct: MFA is defined by combining factors from different categories. A password is 'Something You Know'; a smartphone push approval is 'Something You Have'. Using both satisfies the MFA requirement because they come from two distinct factor categories.
wrong: Two separate passwords are both 'Something You Know' — the same factor category. Using two factors from the same category does NOT constitute MFA; it only increases password complexity.
Two steps alone do not make MFA. Both steps could be 'Something You Know' (password + PIN). MFA requires the steps to come from different factor categories.
MFA does NOT require biometrics. Any combination of two or more factors from different categories (Know + Have, Have + Are, Know + Are) satisfies MFA.

questions.q: A security analyst is reviewing wireless protocols in use across the organization. Which statement about wireless security protocols is ACCURATE?
options: WEP is the strongest current Wi-Fi encryption standard and should be used for sensitive networks
WPA2 uses the TKIP cipher, which was designed to replace the broken RC4 stream cipher
WPA3 uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) to replace the Pre-Shared Key handshake
WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) is recommended for enterprise wireless deployments
questions.note: WPA3 replaced the WPA2-Personal Pre-Shared Key (PSK) 4-way handshake with SAE, which is resistant to offline dictionary attacks even if the attacker captures the handshake. WEP is broken (RC4 key reuse), WPA2 uses AES-CCMP (not TKIP by default in current deployments), and WPS has a known PIN brute-force vulnerability (CVE-2011-5053).

explain.correct: WPA3-Personal replaced the WPA2 PSK 4-way handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE), derived from the Dragonfly key exchange. SAE provides forward secrecy and resists offline password dictionary attacks.
wrong: WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) was deprecated in 2004 and is cryptographically broken due to weak RC4 key scheduling — an attacker can crack WEP in minutes by capturing ~40,000 packets. It must never be used.
WPA2 uses AES-CCMP as its primary encryption cipher in current deployments. TKIP was a transitional fix used in original WPA (not WPA2) to patch WEP's RC4 weakness without requiring new hardware.

WPS has a documented PIN brute-force vulnerability — the 8-digit PIN is verified in two halves, reducing the attack space to 11,000 combinations. WPS should be disabled, especially in enterprise environments.

questions.q: A hospital assigns all nurses the same access to patient records based on their job role, rather than letting individual employees set their own permissions. Which access control model is the hospital using?
options: Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
Rule-Based Access Control
questions.note: RBAC assigns permissions to roles (Nurse, Doctor, Admin) rather than to individuals. Users inherit permissions by being assigned to a role. This enforces least privilege at scale and is the dominant model in enterprise and healthcare environments.

explain.correct: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) ties permissions to job roles, not individual identities. All users in the 'Nurse' role get the same access set. This enforces least privilege and simplifies administration in large organizations.
wrong: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) lets the resource OWNER decide who gets access — for example, a file owner sharing their file with another user. Access is at the owner's discretion, not set by job role.

Mandatory Access Control (MAC) uses system-enforced sensitivity labels (e.g., Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) and clearance levels to control access. Users cannot change these labels. It is used primarily in government/military systems.

Rule-Based Access Control uses system-defined rules (e.g., firewall ACLs, time-of-day restrictions) to grant or deny access — it is policy-driven, not role-driven, and is different from RBAC despite the similar name.

questions.q: A security technician is hardening a Windows 11 workstation. Which statement about Windows OS hardening controls is CORRECT?
options: BitLocker Full-Disk Encryption stores its recovery key in the TPM by default, with no option to use a PIN
AppLocker is a blacklisting tool that blocks known-malicious executables identified by antivirus signatures
UAC (User Account Control) runs all processes with full administrative privileges to prevent permission errors
AppLocker can restrict which executables, scripts, and installer packages are permitted to run based on publisher, path, or file hash
questions.note: AppLocker is an APPLICATION WHITELISTING tool — it defines what IS allowed to run (by publisher certificate, file path, or hash), blocking everything else by default. This is the opposite of blacklisting. BitLocker uses TPM to store the Volume Master Key but can additionally require a PIN (TPM+PIN mode).

explain.correct: AppLocker enforces application whitelisting by allowing only executables, scripts, MSI packages, and DLLs that match defined rules (publisher, path, or SHA-256 hash). Anything not explicitly permitted is blocked by default.
wrong: BitLocker can use TPM-only mode (auto-unlock) OR TPM+PIN mode for additional protection. The TPM stores the Volume Master Key (VMK), but administrators commonly add a PIN as a second factor for pre-boot authentication.

AppLocker is a WHITELISTING tool, not a blacklisting tool. It defines what IS permitted to run. Blacklisting (blocking known-bad items) is the approach used by traditional antivirus — whitelisting is far more restrictive and secure.

UAC does the OPPOSITE — it ensures processes run with the LOWEST necessary privilege (standard user token) and prompts for elevation only when administrative actions are explicitly requested. Running everything as admin violates least privilege.

questions.q: A company is decommissioning old storage media. The security team must select the correct NIST 800-88 destruction method for each device. Which statement is ACCURATE?
options: Degaussing is effective for sanitizing both HDDs and SSDs because it destroys all magnetic fields
NIST 800-88 'Clear' involves physically shredding media into small particles to prevent data recovery
Cryptographic Erase (CE) renders SSD data unrecoverable by destroying the encryption key that protects the data
Overwriting a modern SSD seven times with random data guarantees complete data sanitization per NIST 800-88
questions.note: NIST SP 800-88 Rev.1 explicitly states that degaussing is INEFFECTIVE on SSDs and flash media (no magnetic storage). For SSDs, Cryptographic Erase — destroying or changing the media encryption key — is the recommended Purge-level method, rendering all encrypted data permanently unrecoverable without physically destroying the drive.

explain.correct: Cryptographic Erase (CE) is NIST 800-88's recommended Purge method for self-encrypting drives and SSDs. By destroying or regenerating the Data Encryption Key (DEK), all encrypted data on the device becomes permanently unreadable — no key, no data.
wrong: Degaussing destroys data by exposing magnetic media to a strong magnetic field. It is ONLY effective on magnetic media (HDDs, magnetic tape). SSDs and flash storage have NO magnetic properties, so degaussing has zero effect on SSD data.

NIST 800-88 'Clear' means overwriting data using software techniques (e.g., writing zeros) to a point where simple recovery tools cannot reconstruct it. Physical shredding is the 'Destroy' method — the highest level of sanitization.

NIST 800-88 Rev.1 explicitly states that traditional overwrite methods are NOT reliable for SSDs due to wear-leveling and over-provisioning — the controller may retain data in spare blocks that overwrite commands never reach. Cryptographic Erase or physical destruction is recommended for SSDs.

questions.q: A security architect is designing a data protection strategy. She uses AES-256 to encrypt stored files and RSA-2048 to securely exchange the AES key between parties. Which statement BEST describes why this hybrid approach is used?
options: AES is asymmetric and uses two keys (public/private), making it ideal for bulk data encryption
RSA is faster than AES for large files, so RSA encrypts the data while AES protects the key
AES is a symmetric cipher (one shared key, very fast) and RSA is asymmetric (key pair, slower) — RSA securely transmits the AES key without sharing it in plaintext
Both AES and RSA are hashing algorithms that verify data integrity rather than providing confidentiality
questions.note: Hybrid encryption is the industry standard (used in TLS, PGP, S/MIME). AES-256 is symmetric — one key encrypts and decrypts, making it fast for bulk data but requiring a secure key exchange. RSA-2048 is asymmetric — the recipient's public key encrypts the AES session key; only the recipient's private key can decrypt it, solving the key distribution problem.

explain.correct: This hybrid model solves both problems: AES-256 (symmetric) encrypts bulk data quickly using a shared session key. RSA-2048 (asymmetric) encrypts and transmits that session key securely — only the holder of the RSA private key can recover it. TLS uses this exact pattern.
wrong: AES is SYMMETRIC — it uses a single shared key for both encryption and decryption. RSA is the asymmetric algorithm that uses a public/private key pair. These definitions are reversed in this option.

RSA is significantly SLOWER than AES for bulk data because of the mathematical complexity of modular exponentiation with large primes. That is precisely why RSA is used only to encrypt the small AES key, not the actual data.

AES and RSA are ENCRYPTION algorithms that provide confidentiality — they transform plaintext into ciphertext. Hashing algorithms (SHA-256, SHA-3) produce a fixed-length digest for integrity verification but are not reversible and do not encrypt data.
